text: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand? 9 points by rzk 2 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 13 comments I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-meta-and-i-never-felt-share-7517317918666211328-7C8N > I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too? How are you handling this? pinscope_dev 2 hours ago | next [–] I had same problem, but after a while I just accepted that is inevitable reply polski-g 19 minutes ago | parent | next [–] "This code is really ugly." That sucks. Ship it. reply mattbrewsbytes 32 minutes ago | prev | next [–] It feels like another layer of "conceptual compression". I'm not sure who/when that phrase came around but in context of Rails is where I heard it and its things like ActiveRecord or really any ORM. You aren't writing the SQL directly, something else is and for the most part it works. Then it doesn't work or your database grows too much and you need to optimize table structures with indexes, etc. My point is if you don't understand the fundamentals of the underlying code (SQL in the example above), you're more likely to have issues in the future. Or maybe not if that app doesn't reach a usage pattern or complexity where the nuances under the hood matter. It really depends on what you're shipping. Meta ships social media apps where in the grand scheme of things if something is broken software wise it largely doesn't matter. What's the worst case? lost ad revenue? Users can't do things? If that were software for MRI machines or aerospace where software issues/bugs can result in lives lost then it matters much more in understanding what is going on at all levels of the software and potentially hardware. reply spacedcowboy 2 hours ago | prev | next [–] I’m slowly coming around to the idea that if it works, I’m good with that. I never used to personally check all my colleagues work, either, I just trusted that they’d done a good job. That’s not to say I blindly trust an LLM - my project is an autovectorising compiler. I have it write a bazillion tests, and I have real, non-trivial programs that it compiled. I have it run a ‘gate’ before releases that takes literally hours on 5 different architectures. To say this code is tested is … masterful understatement. I think what helps is a long planning session, going into details, working out corner cases, designing test-cases, you know work and effort. Once that’s done it’s easier to let it work through the night and do a major production feature. I still review the code, but hand on heart I couldn’t say I’d reviewed everything , sometimes I miss something in a complicated check-in. I try to keep checkins small and contained, but sometimes that’s not easy to manage alongside the “don’t break stuff” rule as well. So it comes down to: I’ve been working on this for 6 months or so, and so far this has worked out for me. You know, kind of like getting used to a colleague’s idiosyncrasies over a period of time. I will say that in my experience the code quality is fairly high. Maybe that’s down to the effort put in ahead of time in the planning stages, I don’t know, but I don’t seem to suffer from the ‘slop’ that people complain of. YMMV. reply yulaow 2 hours ago | parent | next [–] I am not in META but for what I read on blind, assuming it is true, they are not spending any time in long planning sessions or in getting into details of the implementation plan at all, and they could not anymore considering how many PRs in parallel they are requested to manage reply spacedcowboy 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] Yeah, I'm retired. The only person I have to answer to regarding progress is me. I'm a stubborn son of a bitch when it comes to choosing quality over speed... That doesn't mean I don't like progress mind :) This morning I got the preliminary results of a 'C' front-end to the compiler (it uses clang to compile to LLVM IR, then translates to our IR, then feeds that IR into the autovectoriser as if it had parsed the code itself). So for the exact same source code I now have: ┌─────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────┐ │ Benchmark │ clang -O2 │ xcc --par-auto (GPU) │ Speed-up │ ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤ │ saxpy │ 1,546 µs │ 726 µs │ 2.1× │ ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤ │ Mandelbrot │ 394,238 µs │ 2,110 µs │ 187× │ ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤ │ nbody │ 37,090 µs │ 1,035 µs │ 36× │ ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤ │ perlin │ 78,016 µs │ 1,850 µs │ 42× │ ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤ │ mandel_deep │ 73.2 s │ 55.8 ms │ 1,312× │ └─────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────┘ Those are some pretty fine speedups, from naive C, with no alterations from the standard "C" code - it automatically finds places that can be made data-parallel, tracks the data-hazards to make sure its safe to "GPU" and writes all the kernels, boilerplate and data-stream-management if necessary. Obviously the checksums have to match, so I know it did the work correctly too :) Hacker News isn't interested - any post I make linking to the webpages is immediately blocked/dead so I'll wait until the C++ front-end is ready (some time next week) and announce it somewhere else. A compiler that takes standard C/C++ code and speeds it up by automatically finding data-parallel areas and scheduling them on the GPU with no programming overhead is pretty rare. Oh, and it manages the local network as well, so you can run xcd on machines on your lan, or via the TB4/5 bridge between Macs and it'll schedule on other GPUs, just like it manages multiple GPUs on the local machine. It characterises both latency and compute-time to figure out which devices are worth scheduling on. reply pluc 2 hours ago | prev | next [–] The solution is more AI. Throw another agent in to watch your logs, then throw in another agent to watch that agent. Quality is no longer an objective. If it breaks, rebuild it and tell it not to break. reply ORDINAND_PIZZA 2 hours ago | parent | next [–] wow, “quality is no longer an objective” is a wild idea that feels dangerously negligent. quality is all we have, it’s what makes us different from these agents. quality is perplexing to agents because it requires a strange loop into asking why. there’s not always a clear answer. but i think the power is in the ambiguity. if we don’t know why (or don’t care) then what happens if we all adopt this attitude at scale? reply pluc 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] The entire industry is dangerously negligent, we just have better tools and stronger incentives now.
